title: With Due Respect (Vol. 5) -- Ch. 8: Squandering the People's Trust
keywords: an all-knowing God to judge him
Comelec Chair Jose A. R. Melo
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5) -- CJP's January 10, 2010 Inquirer column charging that the Melo-led Comelec had 'regretfully been squandering the people's trust' months before the first automated polls, with preparations 'spotty' and recent decisions 'grossly erroneous and impressed with grave abuse of discretion'

His catalogue of automation red flags -- admitted delays in 'physical' preparations and teacher training, only 30 of 600 sample ballots read at the Smartmatic warehouse, an oversized ballot with too few slots for the candidates, and a '1,630 towns' logistics 'nightmare' of distinct ballots and machines

His critique of the Comelec's 'inexplicable decisions' -- the 'monstrosity' unseating Gov. Grace Padaca, the disqualification of Ang Ladlad on 'wobbly religious and gender grounds,' and the disparate treatment of Brig. Gen. Danilo Lim and Col. Ariel Querubin (an equal-protection violation)

His sober conclusion that, with the May 10 polls four months away and 'no timely solutions in sight,' the Comelec 'has come up short in both its automation work and quasi-judicial decisions' -- so 'it is time to prepare for manual elections'
sub_topics: From credibility to doubt: Melo's appointment 'two years ago' had 'restored credibility' despite objections over his age (76) and 'closeness to the Macapagal family,' and CJP had endorsed him and his automation program -- reminding him that 'beyond the appointing authority, there is media... history... a grateful nation... and an all-knowing God to judge him'

The charge: in recent months the Comelec 'has regretfully been squandering the people's trust,' with events shaking confidence in automation and decisions that are 'grossly erroneous and impressed with grave abuse of discretion'

Spotty preparations: Chair Melo himself admitted 'unnerving delays' in 'physical' preparations -- ballot-box delivery, the ballots' condition, the final candidate list for printing, election-day substitutions -- while teacher orientation and training were 'put on hold'

The failed test: Commissioner Larrazabal reported that of 600 sample ballots tested at the Smartmatic warehouse in Cabuyao, 'only 30 were properly read,' blamed on a 'high shading threshold' said to be 'easily corrected' -- which CJP calls 'unacceptable'

The crowded ballot: a sample ballot (24 by 8.5 inches) had room for only 259 candidate slots (10 president, 10 VP, 40 senators, 199 party-list) against 583 who had filed -- so about 324 'would be eased out,' sure to 'flood the poll body with... complaints'

The logistics 'nightmare': with 1,630 towns each having a distinct local slate, there would be 'at least 1,630 types of ballots' and '1,630 different kinds of voting machines' to deliver precinct-correct -- an 'untested logistical nightmare,' worsened because the Comelec had not posted the ballots online (ehope2010) as he urged, since it 'has not finished cleaning up the candidates' list'

Inexplicable quasi-judicial decisions: citing a 'stinging' Inquirer editorial accusing the body of 'partisanship,' CJP faults the 'monstrosity' decision unseating Gov. Grace Padaca of Isabela (so flimsy that GMA's lawyer Macalintal safely bragged he'd quit practice if the Court affirmed it), the ouster of Ang Ladlad from the party-list on 'wobbly religious and gender grounds' (risking reversal), and the disqualification of Brig. Gen. Danilo Lim while accepting Col. Ariel Querubin though both were detained for breaking their military oaths -- 'a violation of his right to equal protection'

The verdict: the Comelec 'has come up short in both its automation work and quasi-judicial decisions' and 'must work seven times more'; though CJP does 'not doubt the noble intentions of Chairman Melo and Commissioner Sarmiento,' 'the time for automation is running out,' so 'it is time to prepare for manual elections'

stances.claim: Months before the first automated polls, the Melo Comelec was 'squandering the people's trust': preparations were admittedly 'spotty' (ballot delays, a failed warehouse test, an overcrowded ballot, and a '1,630 towns' logistics nightmare), undermining confidence that automation could work.
stances.rhetorical_move: evidence-stacking: piling concrete preparation failures to justify alarm

stances.claim: The Comelec's recent quasi-judicial decisions were 'grossly erroneous and impressed with grave abuse of discretion' -- the Padaca 'monstrosity,' the Ang Ladlad ouster on 'wobbly religious and gender grounds,' and the unequal treatment of Lim and Querubin -- eroding confidence further.
stances.rhetorical_move: parallel indictment: faulting adjudication alongside logistics to show institution-wide failure

stances.claim: With the polls four months away and 'no timely solutions in sight,' the Comelec 'has come up short' and 'must work seven times more' -- and prudence now means it is 'time to prepare for manual elections.'
stances.rhetorical_move: contingency-call: urging a fallback rather than trusting unproven assurances

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's January 10, 2010 Inquirer column, charges that the Melo-led Comelec had 'regretfully been squandering the people's trust' just months before the country's first automated polls. Melo's appointment had once 'restored credibility' despite objections over his age and 'closeness to the Macapagal family,' and CJP had backed him and his automation drive -- reminding him that 'beyond the appointing authority' lie 'media... history... a grateful nation... and an all-knowing God to judge him.' But recent events, he writes, had shaken his confidence: Melo admitted 'unnerving delays' in 'physical' preparations (ballot boxes, ballot condition, the candidate list, election-day substitutions) and teacher training was 'on hold'; only 30 of 600 sample ballots were read at the Smartmatic warehouse (blamed on a 'high shading threshold'); a 24-by-8.5-inch ballot had room for only 259 slots against 583 filed candidates, leaving about 324 'eased out'; and with 1,630 towns each having a distinct slate, there would be 'at least 1,630 types of ballots' and machines to deliver -- 'an untested logistical nightmare,' worsened because the Comelec had not posted the ballots online as he urged, having 'not finished cleaning up the candidates' list.' He then faults the body's 'inexplicable' decisions -- citing a 'stinging' Inquirer editorial on its 'partisanship' -- the 'monstrosity' unseating Gov. Grace Padaca (so flimsy GMA's lawyer Macalintal safely bragged he'd quit if the Court affirmed it), the ouster of Ang Ladlad on 'wobbly religious and gender grounds,' and the disqualification of Brig. Gen. Danilo Lim while accepting Col. Ariel Querubin though both were detained for breaking their military oaths -- 'a violation of his right to equal protection.' The Comelec, he concludes, 'has come up short in both its automation work and quasi-judicial decisions' and 'must work seven times more'; though he does 'not doubt the noble intentions' of Melo and Sarmiento, 'the time for automation is running out,' so 'it is time to prepare for manual elections.'
